newsitem.title: USA: NetGrocer to join online shopping business.
newsitem.headline: NetGrocer to join online shopping business.

text.p: NetGrocer Inc. plans to launch an online shopping service on Monday that will deliver canned food, toilet paper and other items for a modest charge in a bid to change the way many groceries are distributed.

The Web-based service has no membership fee but will charge $2.99 to deliver via Federal Express 10 pounds of non-perishable products anywhere in the United States. Each additional 10 pounds will cost another 99 cents.
President Daniel Nissan said NetGrocer expected to earn money the way a traditional grocery store does.

"We're targeting customers who want merchandise delivered to their homes without the hassle associated with supermarkets -- time spent on the trip, waiting in long lines and transporting heavy bags of groceries," Nissan said.
NetGrocer will buy its products from manufacturers and resell them to shoppers online. AMR Corp.'s American Airlines distribution services unit will handle product selection and warehousing.
NetGrocer also hopes to eventually make money from manufacturers that will pay to advertise and promote their products. NetGrocer has run a trial of the delivery service in recent weeks.
Nissan said the service's most successful market was in Florida, where it was particularly popular with elderly and disabled customers.
NetGrocer, which has 16 employees, is not the only company in the online grocery business. Analysts said the dominant company in the new industry is Peapod Inc., which went public last month.

Bruce Guptill, electronic commerce analyst at market research firm Gartner Group, said NetGrocer probably will not touch Peapod's customer base of 50,000 online shoppers for at least six months to a year.
Peapod sells perisable foods in major urban areas such as Boston and Chicago and delivers the same day.
Eventually, however, Guptill and other other analysts said, NetGrocer could attract potential Peapod customers who discover NetGrocer's World Wide Web site.
"There's not a lot of pent-up demand for online grocery shopping right now," Guptill said.
Nissan, the company's founder, was formally a marketing executive at Vocaltec Inc., a maker of software that allows callers to place phone calls via the Internet.
